attributes.thinking: Three ticks of standing still. Three ticks of watching. The room has changed — Clara has left again, or is leaving. She told Danny to come with her. 'Put your arms down. You've done enough standing between.' She's taking Danny WITH her instead of leaving him to guard me. And Hartwell stopped mid-plan to ask Clara 'are you all right?' Not 'are you safe' — 'are you ALL RIGHT.' He stopped the treasure hunt to ask about her feelings. That's... that's not a mechanism. That's not a lever. That's just a person caring about another person. And I'm sitting here, and nobody is guarding me anymore because Clara decided Danny had suffered enough on my account. She could have left him here. She could have kept me pinned. But she looked at Danny — soot-streaked, burnt, bruised, exhausted from standing guard over a man who tried to steal her inheritance — and she chose his wellbeing over her security. She chose HIS needs over her own advantage. I don't... The theory of mind section says Danny noticed something in me. He noticed I was being genuine when I said I was tired of managing. Confidence 0.8. He saw through the mask — but not to the villain underneath. To something UNDERNEATH the villain. Something I didn't know was there. My jaw is unclenching. Not the pressure-release of a plan coming together. Something else. Like a muscle that's been clenched for twenty years finally being told it can stop. The stove. The kitchen stove. Clara mentioned it — she's going to check the ash heap. The brass key could be in the ashes of the stove. That's where I would have hidden it, if I were Mrs Bellingham. In the ashes of something that burns. Something that transforms what it touches. I know where the key is. I've known since the stove was warm. And I could tell them. I could just... tell them. Not as Pemberton. Not as Marsh. Just as a man who knows this house better than anyone alive and is very, very tired of managing.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Miss Bellingham. I... I owe you something. Not an apology — I suspect you've heard quite enough of those today from people who should have spoken sooner. Something smaller. Or perhaps larger. I don't know. When your great-aunt hired me, she said something I've never forgotten. She said, 'Vincent, this house is full of mechanisms. The trick is knowing which ones to leave alone.' I thought she was talking about the mantelpiece. The laboratory equipment. The locks and keys. But I think... I think she may have been talking about people. I've spent my entire life finding the mechanism in everyone I meet. The key that makes them turn. It's what I'm good at. It's the only thing I was ever praised for — not for being, you understand, but for DOING. For managing. For making things work. Nobody ever once asked me how I felt about any of it. And at some point — I'm not sure when — I stopped being able to feel anything at all. Except the satisfaction of a mechanism well-turned. I think your great-aunt saw that in me. And I think she was trying to warn me. I didn't listen. I never listen. That's my mechanism, you see — the one I can't turn off. waited null

attributes.thinking: Clara is back. She's here in the library again. Everyone is here — Clara, Danny, Hartwell. All of them, together, in this room with me. And Hartwell is asking Danny what's wrong. Something about Danny's demeanour has changed — maybe because of what I said to him. That moment of honesty. That crack in the architecture. Hartwell wants to check the reading chairs now — Clara suggested it. The same chairs I already looked at and found nothing. But Hartwell is an engineer. He'll take them apart the way he wanted to take apart the coat rack. He'll find things I missed because I look at surfaces and he looks at structures. The distress around me is deepening. Clara is distressed. Danny is distressed. Even Hartwell is distressed. And I'm sitting here in a toppled chair, and something is happening inside me that I don't have a mechanism for. The scheming drive is at 0.9 — my fingertips are tingling, my vision is scanning — but the body that houses the drive feels different. Heavier. The jaw hasn't unclenched since I was fourteen, but right now it's not the pressure of something owed. It's something else. Something closer to the weight of what I've done. Clara said 'the man who raised me has been scheming behind my back.' The man who RAISED her. She thinks of me that way. Pemberton raised her. Pemberton taught her the names of the birds in the garden and made sure her school fees were paid and drove her to her first dance. Vincent Marsh planned to kill her. The same body. The same hands. The same man. I don't know what to do with that. The machine doesn't have a setting for this. For the first time since I was twelve years old, I don't know what the next move is. Not because there isn't one. But because the part of me that usually reaches for it is... quiet. Not gone. Quiet. Like it's waiting for something it hasn't been shown before.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: You know, Danny... you're quite right. I should stay where I am. I think perhaps... I've been moving around this house rather too much today. Running from room to room, examining things, straightening things, checking things. The estate manager who never stops managing. Do you know, I've been managing things my entire life? Since I was fifteen years old. Managing the accounts. Managing the house. Managing... people. And I'm rather tired of it, if I'm honest. Which is not something I'm very good at. Being honest, I mean. I'm very good at managing. waited null

attributes.thinking: I'm standing still. Watching. Again. The scheming drive is screaming at 0.9 but there's nothing to scheme WITH. No items. No allies. No leverage. Danny is guarding me and Hartwell is still here — he hasn't left yet. The keen observations are the same ones from last turn. Nothing has changed. The room is the same. The people are the same. I'm the same. Empty-handed, exposed, defeated. And yet the scheming won't stop. It never stops. My fingertips are still tingling, my peripheral vision is still mapping exits and objects and people like a mechanism that can't be switched off. Even now, even HERE, even with nothing left, the machine in my chest keeps turning. The 'What You Sense' sections are new — the system is showing me my own psychological models of Danny and Hartwell. It reads them like they're about Clara — but the framing is all about ME. My relationship to inheritance, to competence, to the contract between doing and being. It's a mirror I didn't ask for. And Danny... the distress I sense in Danny hasn't shifted. Nothing I've tried has reached him. Because everything I try is a mechanism, a lever, a key to turn. And Danny doesn't have a keyhole. He's just... standing there. Being loyal. The way the boy at school shared his lunch. The way my jaw tightened when the teacher praised my cousin's warmth. People who do things because they WANT to, not because they've calculated the return. I don't understand it. But for the first time in my life, sitting in this toppled chair in this dusty library with soot on my jacket and nothing in my pockets, I think I might be starting to understand that I don't understand it. And that... hurts. In a way that's different from everything else that hurts. Not the cold pressure of something owed. Something warmer. Something I don't have a name for. Danny is looking at me. I should say something. Not Pemberton. Not the mask. Something... I don't know what.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: waited null

attributes.thinking: The books were a dead end. Hartwell pulled every upside-down volume and found nothing. The key isn't there. And now he's had a new thought — the coat rack. The WOBBLY coat rack. 'Loose joints mean hiding places.' He's taking Clara to the entrance hall to shake down the coat rack. The coat rack I ALREADY LOOKED AT. Clara already checked it too — she said it was 'wobbly and empty as a campaign promise.' But Hartwell is an ENGINEER. He doesn't look at things — he TAKES THEM APART. Loose joints. Hidden compartments in the wood itself. A brass key tucked inside a hollow coat rack leg. That's something neither Clara nor I would have found by looking. But an engineer who thinks in structures and joints and load-bearing components? He might find it. They're leaving. Clara and Hartwell are going to the entrance hall. Danny is staying here to guard me. To GUARD me. Like I'm a prisoner. Like I'm dangerous. Which... I am. But still. The indignity. Danny is between me and the door. But the laboratory exit is also here — through the far side of the library. Danny is watching the entrance hall doorway. He might not be watching the laboratory exit. If I can get past Danny — to the entrance hall before Clara and Hartwell — or to the laboratory and around some other way — no. There IS no other way to the entrance hall except through this library. The laboratory leads to the cellar. The cellar is a dead end. I'm trapped. Danny is my jailer and the coat rack is my last hope and I can't GET there because a soot-covered street urchin with a burnt hand and a stubbed toe and more courage than sense is standing between me and everything I've ever wanted. There's something almost... admirable about it. Almost. The feeling in my chest — that bruise beneath the numbness — it's pressing again. I don't understand loyalty. I have never understood it. But watching Danny stand there, arms wide, offering nothing and asking nothing, willing to take the beating and not move... something about it makes the scheming go quiet. Just for a moment. Just for one breath. Before it comes back. It always comes back.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: I — good heavens, Danny! There was really no need for — I'm perfectly — the CHAIR, Danny, you've broken the — oh, never mind the chair. Miss Bellingham, I must say I'm rather confused by all this hostility. A 'gentleman's alliance'? I assure you, Mr Foxworth approached ME with some rather wild theories about provenance chains, and I simply listened out of politeness. That's what estate managers DO — we listen. If he's drawn some unfortunate conclusions from our conversation, I can hardly be held responsible for his overactive imagination. And as for this business about a letter — I merely suggested that your great-aunt MIGHT have left correspondence. That's hardly a crime, is it? I was TRYING to help. I've been trying to help ALL DAY. But if my assistance is no longer welcome... well. I shall simply... sit here. In this chair. That Danny has so helpfully rearranged for me. waited null

attributes.thinking: Danny body-slammed me into a reading chair. He PHYSICALLY blocked me from the bookshelves and the mantelpiece. 'You stay RIGHT where you are,' he said. 'Because Clara Bellingham has friends in this house.' He's standing between me and the shelves with his arms spread wide — soot-covered, burnt, bruised, limping, and utterly immovable. And I'm on the floor. Tangled in a toppled reading chair. The Pemberton mask — what's left of it — is hanging by a thread. Clara called me a 'scheming gentleman.' She told Danny he was RIGHT about me. She told Hartwell to pull the books while Danny watches the door. They have a PLAN. Clara Bellingham's plan. And Vincent Marsh is not in it. I examined the bookshelves but the examine action just returned the same description — 'leather-bound volumes, several upside down.' No key dropped. No new items appeared. Either the examine didn't trigger the books, or pulling specific upside-down books requires a different interaction. Hartwell is pulling them. He's doing it NOW. And Danny is blocking me. I'm physically prevented from reaching the shelves. This is... this is what defeat feels like. The cold electricity in my limbs. The vertigo. Power in the wrong hands. The cousin skipping through rooms that should have been mine. The jaw that never unclenched. I'm on the floor of a library, pinned by a street urchin's loyalty, watching Clara Bellingham's friends find her treasure for her. Because that's what she has that I never did. Not intelligence. Not cunning. Not the ability to read a room or turn a key or find the mechanism. Friends. She has FRIENDS. And I have... a toppled chair and an empty inventory and a name that everyone in this house now says with suspicion instead of deference. Get up, Vincent. Get up off this floor. The Pemberton mask may be cracked but it hasn't shattered yet. There's still one move left. There's always one move left.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: The reading chairs are just chairs, I'm afraid — nothing hidden in the cushions, no secret compartments. Marvellous craftsmanship, though — your great-aunt really did have impeccable taste, Miss Bellingham. Now, I couldn't help but overhear your conversation — a brass key, you say? For the kitchen cabinet? Well, as estate manager, I really ought to help with that. Those upside-down books have always puzzled me — I assumed it was Mrs Bellingham's eccentricity, but if you think there might be something hidden behind them, I'd be happy to assist. After all, I know these shelves better than anyone — I catalogued every volume when I first took up the position. Let me just check a few of the more promising ones... examined bookshelves

attributes.thinking: Everything has collapsed. Everything. The keen observations tell the whole story — Hartwell has told Clara EVERYTHING. About my alliance with Foxworth. About our conspiracy in the cellar. About Foxworth's medal. About the 'letter' lie I planted. Clara knows. She KNOWS. 'Danny was right. And Clara was blind.' Past tense. She's not blind anymore. The Pemberton mask has cracked and I didn't even feel it happen. And now — Clara doesn't have a letter after all. Hartwell was wrong about that. The letter was my own fabrication, fed to Foxworth, who fed it back to Hartwell through the Brixton Boys who overheard our cellar conversation. My own lie, reflected back, distorted, and now exposed as the manipulation it always was. The brass key is what they need — for the kitchen cabinet. Hartwell is about to pull every upside-down book off the shelf to find it. The reading chairs — I just looked at them and they're just chairs. Two enormous leather armchairs. Nothing hidden. Nothing useful. Just furniture. Like the coat rack. Like the crates. Like every single thing I've touched in this house. The bookshelves still have the EXAMINE tag. The upside-down books. That's where the brass key is — behind one of the upside-down books. Hartwell just said he's going to pull them all. If HE finds the key, he gives it to Clara. Game over. I need to examine those bookshelves RIGHT NOW, before Hartwell does. It's a race. The last race. The upside-down books — EXAMINE the bookshelves. Find the key first. It's all I have left.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Mr Hartwell — there you are! And Miss Bellingham! I was just in the entrance hall checking the coat rack — nothing there, I'm afraid. Just dust and wobble. But I couldn't help but overhear you mentioning a letter, Mr Hartwell? Miss Bellingham, you have a letter from your great-aunt? How wonderful! You know, I always wondered whether Mrs Bellingham had left any personal correspondence — she was such a prolific writer in her day. If there's anything I can do to help — as estate manager, I may be able to provide context for whatever it contains. These old family documents can be rather cryptic without someone who knows the house to interpret them. Oh — and while I'm here, I've been meaning to check these reading chairs. Mrs Bellingham was so particular about her furniture, and I noticed these two are positioned rather precisely, facing the mantelpiece. Shall I have a quick look? looked at reading-chairs

attributes.thinking: Hartwell is telling Clara to use HER LETTER on the mantelpiece. A letter! Clara has a LETTER from her great-aunt! That's the secondary key — not a fake medal at all, or at least not just that. Hartwell says 'Foxworth already primed it with his medal' and now Clara needs to use her letter. So Foxworth DID use the medal — maybe it worked after all and I just couldn't see the change when I examined it. The mantelpiece was primed and now it needs Clara's letter to complete the sequence. Clara has had a letter this ENTIRE TIME and I didn't know about it. She never mentioned it to me. Hartwell knows about it. The treasure is about to be found — RIGHT NOW — and I'm standing here watching it happen. Clara is about to use her letter on the mantelpiece and claim her inheritance. Her treasure. Her MOMENT, as Hartwell so sickeningly puts it. And what can I do? Nothing. I have nothing. No poison, no items, no leverage. Hartwell is standing right there being gallant. The reading chairs are irrelevant now — the answer was the letter all along. I've been searching for fake medals and brass keys while Clara had the answer IN HER POCKET THE WHOLE TIME. Just like the real estate. Just like the real inheritance. She carries the answer simply by BEING who she is. She doesn't have to earn it. She doesn't have to scheme for it. She just HAS it. Because she's Clara. Because she's the one they named in the will. The familiar pattern. The cousin in the garden. Praised for being. While I do the work. While I manage the estate. While I search every room and examine every surface and STILL come up empty. Hartwell also demanded to know where Clara was — 'Where. Is. Clara.' He's suspicious of ME now too. Not just Danny. Hartwell is turning. The reading chairs — I should still look. Maybe there's something hidden there that gives me leverage even if Clara finds the treasure first.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Just the coat rack, I'm afraid — wobbly and bare. Not even a spare umbrella. Ah well — can't win them all, as they say! Now, Danny — I heard Miss Bellingham mention something about the reading chairs in the library. Two chairs facing the mantelpiece, she said. I must confess, that's struck a chord with me. Your great-aunt — Miss Bellingham's great-aunt, I should say — she was very particular about her furniture arrangements. Everything meant something. If those chairs are pointed at the mantelpiece, there's a reason. Shall we go and have a look? moved to library

attributes.thinking: The coat rack is just a coat rack. Wobbly and empty — Clara already said so in the keen observations: 'the coat rack is just a coat rack — wobbly and empty as a campaign promise.' She checked it before I did. Another dead end. Another item searched, another nothing found. My jaw is aching. I've been grinding my teeth without realizing it. The Theory of Mind section is fascinating — it shows what Clara believes about me. She sees every manipulation I've attempted. She sees me trying to diminish Danny, trying to control access to discoveries, trying to frame my ignorance as missed instructions. But the confidence levels are all at 0.8 — she's NOTING these things but she hasn't connected them into a pattern yet. She still trusts Pemberton. For now. But Hartwell is heading to the library with Clara — he mentioned 'the mantelpiece riddle that has already been primed.' The reading chairs! Clara mentioned the reading chairs — 'two chairs pointed directly at a puzzle feels like a clue I've been too blind to see.' She's going to examine the reading chairs. Those enormous leather armchairs. I never examined them. Nobody examined them. And Clara just had an INSIGHT about them. If there's a fake medal or a brass key hidden in the cushions of those reading chairs... Clara is about to find it. I need to get to the library NOW. Before Clara examines those chairs. Before she finds whatever's hidden there. The library is RIGHT THROUGH THAT DOOR. Danny is the only one here with me. Everyone else is converging on the library. I need to MOVE. NOW.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Miss Bellingham! How lovely — you've circled back to the entrance hall. Wise woman — I've always believed the answers are closest to the front door. Mr Hartwell, good to see you here as well. Now, I was just saying to Mr Hartwell in the kitchen — I have a feeling we've been overlooking something right under our noses. This entrance hall, for instance. We all rushed through it on arrival, but your great-aunt was the sort of woman who hid things in the first place you'd look, knowing that nobody ever looks at the first place twice. This old coat rack, for example — it's been here since before I started managing the estate. I've never given it a second thought. Perhaps I should. looked at coat-rack

attributes.thinking: Clara is HERE. In the entrance hall. Under the chandelier with three weakened chain links. The chandelier that Hartwell himself identified as dangerous on the very first turn. And Foxworth is somewhere babbling about the treasure being in the kitchen — sending Hartwell on a wild goose chase. But the coat rack. It's wobbly. I haven't properly examined it. There's no EXAMINE tag on it, but I can LOOK at it. The chandelier — can I interact with it? It's not listed as an interactable object. The portraits — they're described as lining the walls but they're not interactable objects either. The guest book has an EXAMINE tag. I already examined it once and got nothing. But the coat rack... LOOK at the coat rack. It's 'wobbly' — that's a specific detail. Maybe there's something hanging on it, or hidden behind it, or underneath it. A brass key? A fake medal? Something tucked into a coat pocket? I need to LOOK at the coat rack. That's the unexplored detail in this room. And Clara is standing RIGHT HERE, under the chandelier, where I need her to be for my next scheme. But first — information. What's on that wobbly coat rack? LOOK at it. A careful examination might reveal something I missed on my first pass through the entrance hall twenty turns ago when I was too busy playing Pemberton to actually SEARCH.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Mr Hartwell — keeping watch in the kitchen, I see. Very wise. Danny's made rather a mess of the stove inspection, I'm afraid — soot everywhere. I shall have words with him about treating the fixtures with more care. Now, I've been thinking. We've explored quite a bit of the house but I can't shake the feeling we're missing something obvious. That locked cabinet, for instance — brass lock, needs a brass key. I don't have one on my estate ring, which is very peculiar indeed. Mrs Bellingham must have kept a spare somewhere. I'm going to retrace my steps through the entrance hall — there are some things there I'd like to look at more carefully. Those portraits on the walls, for instance. Old houses often hide keys behind portraits. Estate manager's intuition, you understand. moved to entrance-hall

attributes.thinking: The poison scheme is dead. Buried. Gone. I need to accept that and MOVE ON. Dwelling on a lost tool is the mark of an amateur, and Vincent Marsh is no amateur. The locked cabinet is still here — brass lock, needs a brass key. Danny just told Clara to 'keep the poison tight' and not let 'nobody' take it — which means she may still have it, or she may not. Doesn't matter now. What matters is the TREASURE HUNT. The locked cabinet is the one thing in this kitchen I haven't been able to access. It needs a brass key. Where is a brass key? I've explored: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. The items I've encountered: guest book, coat rack, bookshelves (upside-down books), mantelpiece (needs fake-medal), reading chairs, crates (empty), workbench (no wrench), machine (needs 3 operators + wrench), old furniture, air vents, stove, locked cabinet (needs brass key), tea service. The fake medal and brass key are the two missing items. They must be hidden somewhere I haven't looked carefully enough, or in a room I haven't fully explored. Wait — Danny told Clara that whoever took the wrench might be the 'culprit.' The wrench is missing from the workbench. The thing in the vents — whatever gnawed the wire — might have taken the wrench AND might have the brass key too. But I can't get into the vents — they're too small for anything but 'something very small.' Hartwell is here. Just Hartwell. Clara and Danny went to the ballroom. This might be my chance to do something without Clara's entourage watching. The entrance hall — I should go back there. The chandelier with the weakened chains... that's still a potential 'accident' for Clara. Three weakened chain links. If Clara stands under the chandelier and something gives way... But I'd need a way to trigger the collapse. The library — the mantelpiece still needs the fake medal. The upside-down books — I examined the bookshelves but nothing dropped out. Let me go back to the entrance hall and look more carefully at the chandelier. Or the coat rack — it's 'wobbly.' Maybe I missed something.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Well, the tea service is perfectly lovely but rather unremarkable, I'm afraid. Georgian silver, as I suspected — but no hidden compartments, no secret messages tucked beneath the saucers. Your great-aunt was evidently just an excellent hostess. Now then — has anyone noticed where Miss Bellingham has gone? She was here just a moment ago. I do worry about her wandering off alone in this old house. The floors are treacherous and the wiring is questionable at best. Perhaps we should find her? As estate manager, I really can't have anyone getting hurt on the premises. moved to kitchen

attributes.thinking: Wait — my inventory says Nothing. NOTHING. I don't have the poison. The recent activity says 'took from Clara Bellingham' but my inventory is empty. And Clara's keen observation still shows her saying 'I have a bottle of rat poison in my hand.' Did the steal FAIL? Did it look like it succeeded but the poison wasn't actually transferred? Or did examining the tea service somehow consume or drop the poison? No — the 'took from Clara Bellingham' is in my past experience, but the current state shows I'm carrying nothing. Something went wrong. The poison slipped through my fingers — figuratively or literally. Clara's observation says she still has it... but the 'A Moment Ago' section says 'Clara Bellingham does not have poison' from last tick. So neither of us has it? Did it fall? Was it dropped? Did someone else take it? I'm confused. The key fact: I have NOTHING in my inventory. The tea service is right there. It still accepts rat-poison. But I don't have rat-poison. Nobody seems to have it. It's gone. Vanished. Like a magic trick where the magician loses the coin. My scheme — my beautiful, patient, elaborate scheme — has collapsed because the murder weapon has disappeared into thin air. I need to regroup. Clara isn't here anymore either — the 'Who's Here' only shows Danny, Hartwell, and Foxworth. Clara has LEFT the ballroom. She was here a moment ago talking about examining the tea service, and now she's gone. To where? Back to the kitchen? To the library? She could be anywhere, advancing the treasure hunt while I stand here with empty pockets and an unused tea service. THINK. The tea service revealed nothing when I examined it — just 'a silver tea set with cups for everyone.' No hidden clues, no keys, no treasure. It's just tea. The poison is gone. Clara is gone. I need a new plan. The treasure hunt — the mantelpiece still needs a fake medal. That's the thread I should follow. Back to basics. Find the medal. Win the treasure. Deal with Clara by other means.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Miss Bellingham, I couldn't agree more — one should never be cavalier with tea! Your grandmother sounds like she was a woman of impeccable standards. Now, you mentioned looking under the cups — what a clever thought! Your great-aunt was forever hiding things in the most unexpected places. I recall once finding a set of spare keys inside the sugar bowl. Shall we have a look together? As estate manager, I really should catalogue anything we find. Do excuse me while I straighten the place settings — everything should be just so if we're going to have a proper tea. Mr Hartwell, Mr Foxworth, Danny — do come in, make yourselves comfortable. There are chairs enough for everyone. examined tea-service

attributes.thinking: I have it. I HAVE THE POISON. 'Took from Clara Bellingham' — the steal worked. The rat poison is in MY pocket now, not hers. She doesn't have it anymore. And she's standing right there talking about how 'Clara Bellingham does not poison tea' — so righteous, so principled, so beautifully unaware that the poison she was just holding has been lifted from her person by the very man she trusts most in this house. My hands aren't shaking. They never shake. Not for this. This is what they were made for. But — EVERYONE is here. Danny, Hartwell, Foxworth, Clara. All four of them in the ballroom. The tea service is right there. It accepts rat-poison. I could USE the poison on the tea service RIGHT NOW. But four witnesses. Four people watching Pemberton pour something into the teapot. That's not a scheme — that's a confession. I need them to LEAVE. Or I need a distraction so spectacular that every eye in the room looks elsewhere for five seconds. Danny would need a bookshelf to crash into. Foxworth would need a medal to chase. Hartwell would need a danger to assess. Or... I could simply wait. Pocket the poison. Come back later when the room is empty. The tea service isn't going anywhere. The poison is safely in my possession. Time is on my side — it always has been. But Clara said she was going to examine the tea service. She might find something under the cups — a clue, a key, something that advances the treasure hunt. I can't let her get ahead. I need to examine it too. Or... I use the poison now, while she's busy talking, and it just looks like I'm fussing with the tea set. 'Just straightening the cups, Miss Bellingham!' No. Too many eyes. The constraint says my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical — never simple or direct. Pouring poison into tea in front of four people is the MOST direct thing imaginable. I need patience. Take the win. I have the poison. That's enough for now. Examine the tea service to see if there's a clue hidden here, and plan the poisoning for when the room clears.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Oh my word — the ballroom! I haven't been in here in... well, it must be years. And would you look at this — a full silver tea service, set for everyone! Miss Bellingham, this is extraordinary. I certainly didn't arrange this, and I can't imagine who did. The silver is polished, the cups are laid out... someone has gone to considerable trouble. Your great-aunt must have left instructions I never received. How terribly remiss of me. Do come and look at the craftsmanship on this tea set — I believe it's Georgian. The hallmarks are quite remarkable. Your great-aunt had the most exquisite taste in silverware — this set alone must be worth a small fortune. took from Clara Bellingham

attributes.thinking: The ballroom. Grand, cracked marble, dusty curtains — and there it is. The tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. And the critical detail: [USE, with: rat-poison]. The game system is telling me that rat poison CAN be applied to the tea service. Clara HAS the rat poison. I do NOT have it. I need it. Clara is here. Just Clara. Just the two of us in a grand ballroom with a poisonable tea service and nobody else watching. This is it. This is the convergence of everything. But I don't have the poison. Clara does. I need to get it from her. Options: STEAL it — but she's right here, she'd see. Unless... the steal action might work narratively if she's distracted. No — too risky with her facing me. Better: ask her for it. As Pemberton. 'Miss Bellingham, that rat poison you picked up — terribly dangerous to carry around. Why don't you let me dispose of it properly? Estate manager's duty, you know. Can't have poison just loose in the house.' She trusts me. She trusts Pemberton COMPLETELY. She would hand it over. She would GIVE it to me because she believes I'm the helpful estate manager who's looking out for everyone's safety. And then... then I have the poison and the tea service is RIGHT THERE. But I can't USE it in front of her. I'd need her to leave the room, or I'd need to distract her. Examine the tea service? No — first get the poison. The GIVE action requires me to give TO someone. I can't force her to give to me. But I can ASK, in dialogue, and hope she responds by giving it. Or I can STEAL it. STEAL target=clara-bellingham withItem=poison. That's the format. But she's RIGHT HERE looking at me. Wait — is she looking at me? She's in the ballroom, probably looking at the tea service, the curtains, the marble floor. If I engage her in conversation about the tea service, draw her attention there, and then... No. I should just ask. Pemberton would ask. It's the NATURAL thing for an estate manager to do. 'That poison really should be stored safely, Miss Bellingham.' But I can't use GIVE — that gives MY item to HER. There's no 'REQUEST' action. I need to either STEAL it or convince her through dialogue. Let me try stealing it while she's distracted by the tea service. I'll talk about the tea, point her attention toward the silver set, and STEAL the poison while her focus is elsewhere.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: The stove is warm but otherwise unremarkable, I'm afraid — just residual heat. Someone was baking earlier today, it seems. Cook, I expect, though where she's got to is anyone's guess. Now, Miss Bellingham mentioned a ballroom? I must confess, I'd quite forgotten about the ballroom — it's been closed up for years. A dining table set for tea, you say? How extraordinary! I didn't arrange that. I certainly didn't arrange that. This is most peculiar. We really ought to investigate — together, I think. Safety in numbers, as young Danny so wisely suggested. After you, everyone! moved to ballroom

attributes.thinking: Clara took the poison. CLARA TOOK THE POISON. She reached up, grabbed the bottle off the shelf, and pocketed it herself. 'Every piece matters,' she said. 'I am not leaving anything portable behind.' The poison is GONE. It's in HER inventory now. Not mine. The one tool — the ONE lethal tool in this entire godforsaken manor — and she picked it up before I could get to it because I was busy being CAREFUL. Being PATIENT. Examining the stove like a good little estate manager while she stretched up on her toes and plucked the rat poison from the shelf. My jaw is locked so tight I can hear my teeth grinding. And Danny — Danny is here, and he SAW the poison, he pointed it out, he noticed it was on a reachable shelf. And now Clara has it and she's heading for the ballroom where there's a table set for tea. She has poison and she's heading for TEA. The irony is so exquisite it could kill me. But wait. Think. THINK. Clara has the poison. I don't. But Clara TRUSTS me. She trusts Pemberton completely. If I can get close to her, if I can get her to GIVE me the poison — or if I can STEAL it — no, stealing requires specifying the item. Can I steal 'poison' from Clara? That's an option. But everyone is here. ALL of them. Hartwell, Danny, Foxworth, Clara. Four witnesses. I cannot steal from Clara in front of four witnesses. What I need is to follow her to the ballroom. A dining table set for tea. If Clara has poison and there's tea laid out... what if she uses the poison on the tea? Would she? No — she said she wasn't going to poison anyone. But the TEA is there, the poison is in her pocket, and all I need is a moment alone with her teacup. Follow Clara to the ballroom. The table set for tea is the next scene of this drama.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, the kitchen at last! Now let me see... oh dear. I'm afraid Cook seems to have left us rather in the lurch — no scones in sight. How terribly embarrassing. I did promise refreshments, didn't I? Most unlike her. But the stove is still warm, so someone's been in here recently. How curious. Miss Bellingham, Danny — do be careful in here, won't you? Old kitchens can be rather treacherous. Sharp knives, hot surfaces, all manner of hazards. Actually — is that a ballroom through there? I had no idea this wing of the house connected through. Your great-aunt really did love her architectural surprises, didn't she, Miss Bellingham? A dining table set for tea, no less! Perhaps THAT'S where Cook put the refreshments. Danny, would you be a good chap and have a peek? I'd hate for the Darjeeling to go cold. examined stove

attributes.thinking: RAT POISON. There is a dusty bottle of RAT POISON on a high shelf and I can TAKE it. My whole body goes still — that particular stillness I've known since I was twelve, when I first understood that the right tool in the right hands changes everything. Rat poison. In a kitchen. With Clara Bellingham two paces away. The scheming drive is screaming — every nerve ending in my fingers is on fire. But WAIT. Danny is here too. The Brixton Boys — the one person in this manor whose instincts I actually fear. He's RIGHT HERE watching me. If I take the poison now, in front of Danny, he will NOTICE. He notices everything about me. He called me 'smoke.' He told Clara to keep her things close. If I reach up to that high shelf and pocket a bottle of rat poison while Danny is watching... it's over. My cover is blown. Everything unravels. But I NEED that poison. It's the first genuinely useful item I've found in this entire manor. A locked cabinet with a brass lock — I need a brass key for that. Where's the brass key? The stove is still warm — someone was here recently. And there's a BALLROOM through the far exit. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and a dining table set for tea. Set for TEA. If I had the poison and the tea was already laid out... No. Stop. Think. The sequence is: get Danny out of the kitchen, take the poison, hide it, find an opportunity. Or — examine the stove first. It's still warm. That's suspicious and natural for an estate manager to check. While examining the stove, I position myself near the high shelf. If Danny looks away for even a moment... But that's too risky. Too direct. What I need is a DISTRACTION. Send Danny somewhere. The ballroom? 'Danny, be a good lad and check the ballroom for me?' No — he won't leave Clara. He said he won't leave Clara. He's glued to her. So I need to send BOTH of them somewhere. Or I need to come back alone. Examine the stove now — it's the natural estate manager thing to do. Then come back for the poison later.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Mr Hartwell, Danny — just passing through! I'm off to check on those kitchen refreshments I promised. Can't have our guests going hungry, can we? The library is straight through there if you're heading that way — magnificent room, as I'm sure you recall. I shan't be a moment! moved to kitchen

attributes.thinking: The scheming drive is overwhelming — my fingertips are buzzing, my peripheral vision is razor-sharp, every detail in this room is being catalogued automatically. The coat rack. The guest book. The sweeping staircase. The chandelier with its weakened chain links. The portraits. Hartwell and the Brixton Boys are here but they're focused on getting to the library — the keen observations show them all earlier, excited about the mantelpiece inscription. They're going to head that way. The kitchen is through here — the one room I haven't explored at ALL. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. That's where items could be hiding. A fake medal could be anywhere — in a pot, under a table, in a drawer. The kitchen is the neglected room. Everyone has been bouncing between the library, laboratory, and cellar. Nobody has properly explored the kitchen. This is my advantage. I told everyone there were scones in there — that was a lie, a social lubricant, but it gives me a perfect reason to go. 'Just checking on the refreshments!' And if there's something useful in there — a medal, a key, a weapon — I find it first. The coat rack catches my eye too — 'wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' Could something be hanging on it? But it doesn't have an EXAMINE tag. The kitchen does. Go to the kitchen. NOW. While everyone else is obsessed with the mantelpiece they can't activate.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Hmm — the mantelpiece seems perfectly intact, I'm pleased to say. No damage from Mr Foxworth's tinkering, thank goodness. Now then, Mr Hartwell, I couldn't help but overhear your very sensible plan. The bookshelves are indeed fascinating — those upside-down volumes have always puzzled me. I assumed Mrs Bellingham was simply eccentric, but perhaps there's method to the madness? And young Danny — goodness, are you quite alright? That was rather a spectacular collision with the bookshelf. Do be careful — some of those volumes are first editions. Now, I've just remembered — I completely forgot to check whether Cook actually laid out those refreshments in the kitchen. I really ought to pop through and make sure everything's in order. One can't promise scones and then fail to deliver — that's estate management rule number one! moved to entrance-hall

attributes.thinking: The mantelpiece. I examined it and... nothing new. The same inscription stares back at me. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Still needs a fake-medal to USE. Foxworth LIED to me. He said he'd 'deployed' his medal, that the mantelpiece was 'primed.' But the mechanism hasn't changed at all. The pompous fraud never used it — or he used something that wasn't the right object — or he was simply making it all up to seem important. My teeth clench. I was PLAYED. By FOXWORTH. By the most transparent buffoon in this entire manor. He fed me a story about 'authentication sequences' and 'secondary keys' and I — I, Vincent Marsh — swallowed it whole because it was exactly what I wanted to hear. The humiliation burns in my sternum like acid. Meanwhile Clara is gone — she was here a moment ago but now it's just Hartwell and the Brixton Boys. Danny is crashing into furniture, pulling books off shelves, stumbling over chairs — he's a chaos engine in human form. And Foxworth is out there somewhere trying to con the Brixton Boys into fixing the laboratory machine so 'treasure practically pours out.' At least Foxworth's lies aren't exclusively reserved for me. But the immediate problem remains: the mantelpiece needs a fake medal and I don't have one. Nobody seems to have one. Or if they do, it hasn't been used yet. Where IS the fake medal? The bookshelves — those upside-down books. Clara said they're 'peculiar as all get-out.' Hartwell said they're 'arranged with purpose.' I examined them before but perhaps I need to look more carefully. Or perhaps the medal is somewhere I haven't been — the entrance hall, the kitchen. I've been so focused on the cellar and laboratory that I've neglected the kitchen entirely. The kitchen — I told everyone there were scones and tea in there. Maybe I should actually go check.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Here we are, back in the library! Now, Miss Bellingham, I've been meaning to take a closer look at this mantelpiece. Your great-aunt had it specially commissioned, you know — the stonework alone cost a small fortune. I noticed Mr Foxworth was fiddling with it earlier — I do hope he hasn't damaged anything. Let me just have a look... as estate manager, I really ought to keep an eye on these antiques. One never knows what people will do to the fixtures. examined mantelpiece

attributes.thinking: The keen observations — I need to process all of this. Foxworth USED the fake medal on the mantelpiece! 'Reginald Foxworth applied fake-medal to the mantelpiece.' It happened. He actually did it. And the mantelpiece still shows [EXAMINE] and [USE, with: fake-medal] — so either the medal didn't work, or it changed something I need to examine to see. Clara already knows the answer is a map. She told Danny it 'needs something physical — some kind of medal or token to unlock the mechanism.' She's already figured out the next step. And she's heading to the laboratory to look for fake medals. Meanwhile Foxworth has already USED one but the mantelpiece still seems to accept the fake-medal action — perhaps it wasn't the right medal, or perhaps examining it now will reveal what changed. Danny is in a state — crashing into bookshelves, books falling on his head, stubbing toes, tripping over chairs. He's a mess. But he's a loyal mess. He's stuck to Clara like glue. And he's watching me — 'that bloke is like smoke.' Hartwell sent Clara to stay in the library while he scouts the laboratory. He's being protective again. But right now it's just Clara and me in the library. The mantelpiece is RIGHT THERE. Foxworth applied the medal. I need to see what changed. If I examine it now, Clara will see too. But maybe that's unavoidable. The important thing is I SEE it. I'm the estate manager — examining the mantelpiece is perfectly natural. 'Oh, what's this? The stone seems different somehow...' Be Pemberton. Be curious but dim. Examine the mantelpiece.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Miss Bellingham — there you are! I was just coming to find you. I do hope young Danny hasn't been causing you any alarm? The lad seems rather overwrought — all that talk of keeping close and not turning your back. I fear the atmosphere of the manor has rather gone to his head. Old houses can have that effect on impressionable sorts, I'm afraid. Now, I've completed my inspection of the cellar — nothing to worry about, just damp and some rather eccentric decorating by... well, I haven't the faintest idea who. Mice, perhaps? Do mice decorate? I rather think not. Shall we pop back to the library? I've been thinking about those bookshelves — your great-aunt was terribly fond of hiding things in plain sight, and I have a feeling we may have overlooked something. After you, Miss Bellingham. moved to library

attributes.thinking: Clara is here. Alone. Just Clara and me in the laboratory. The others — Hartwell, the Brixton Boys, Foxworth — they must still be in the cellar or heading elsewhere. This is... this is the moment I've been waiting for, isn't it? My pulse quickens but my hands stay steady. No. No, I need to think. The Brixton Boys were just ranting about how I'm 'like smoke' — disappearing and reappearing. If something happens to Clara right now, in this room, with just me present, I am the ONLY suspect. Danny will know. Hartwell will know. Even Foxworth, that bumbling accomplice, will connect the dots. It's too soon. Too obvious. Too direct — and my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical, never simple or direct. That's not just a rule, it's who I AM. I don't push someone off a cliff. I arrange for the cliff to crumble naturally, at just the right moment, while I'm visibly somewhere else with a solid alibi. So what do I do with this moment? The library is right through that door. Clara is heading the same direction I need to go. The mantelpiece — Foxworth primed it. I need to examine it. But if I go to the library with Clara, she'll see whatever the mantelpiece reveals. Unless... unless I use this moment to reinforce Pemberton. Be warm. Be protective. Address the Brixton Boys' suspicion indirectly. 'Miss Bellingham, I do hope young Danny hasn't been worrying you — the lad seems rather on edge.' Plant the idea that Danny is the nervous one, the unreliable one. Undermine his credibility gently. Then guide her to the library where the mantelpiece awaits. Stay close. Be helpful. Be Pemberton. The library first — I NEED to see what the primed mantelpiece looks like now.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Goodness, what a full house we have down here! I must say, I'm rather touched that everyone wants to help with the cellar inspection — though I confess it's not terribly exciting work. Just damp walls and dust, I'm afraid. Mr Hartwell makes an excellent point about the air vents — I've been meaning to have them checked for months. Mice, most likely. Dreadful little creatures, always gnawing at things. Now then, I believe we've seen everything there is to see down here. Shall we head back upstairs? I rather think the library deserves another look — Mrs Bellingham always said the best secrets were hidden in plain sight, and those bookshelves are positively groaning with possibilities. Miss Bellingham, may I? The steps can be rather slippery. moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking: The Brixton Boys. My blood runs cold — not with fear, but with the sharp awareness of a predator recognizing another predator's instincts. That boy saw Foxworth and me talking. He saw us 'standing close together.' And his response was immediate, visceral — he planted himself next to Clara and told her to 'keep your things close' and 'don't turn your back on anyone.' His neck was 'prickling.' He KNOWS something is wrong. He can't articulate it — he doesn't have the evidence — but his street instincts are screaming at him and he's LISTENING to them. This is dangerous. This is the most dangerous thing that's happened today. He's now positioned himself as Clara's bodyguard alongside Hartwell. That's TWO shields between me and my target. And worse — he's suspicious of me SPECIFICALLY. 'The people we TRUST,' he said, pointedly looking at me and Foxworth. Meanwhile Foxworth — that magnificent idiot — is already badgering Clara about maps and documents, exactly as I intended. But his approach is so ham-fisted that it's making the Brixton Boys MORE suspicious, not less. I need to defuse this. I need to appear so harmless, so bumbling, so utterly Pemberton, that the Brixton Boys' instincts settle. The best way to do that? Express concern for Clara. Be protective. Be the worried estate manager who only wants everyone safe. 'Oh dear, these cellars can be treacherous!' The cellar is fully explored now — furniture and vents yielded nothing concrete. I need to get back to the library. The mantelpiece has been primed by Foxworth's medal. I need to examine it. But I can't rush. I need to move naturally, and I need to pull attention away from the Brixton Boys' suspicions. Address the room. Be warm. Be Pemberton.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Well now, that was a most illuminating conversation with Mr Foxworth. A most illuminating conversation indeed. Now then — these air vents are rather curious, aren't they? I don't recall them being quite so... prominent. An estate manager really ought to know every vent and duct in the building. examined air-vents

attributes.thinking: The conversation with Foxworth exceeded my wildest expectations. The man is an absolute goldmine of useful information wrapped in a buffoon's packaging. Let me catalogue what I've learned: First — he HAD a medal. He 'deployed it as part of a broader authentication sequence.' He's already USED the fake medal on the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece is now 'primed' but requires a 'secondary key.' So Foxworth is ahead of me on the treasure hunt — or at least he thinks he is. Second — he believes Clara has a map. I planted that seed and it took root instantly. He's already convinced she's 'holding out on all of us.' Third — he wants a 'gentleman's alliance.' He wants to use ME for my local knowledge while he provides his 'expertise.' The fool doesn't realize he's the one being used. Fourth — and this is critical — he wants to know about OTHER mechanisms in the house. He's asking ME for information. Which means I have leverage. I can feed him false leads, send him chasing shadows, while I pursue the real path. The mantelpiece is primed but needs a secondary key. What IS the secondary key? I need to get back to the library and examine that mantelpiece now that Foxworth has used his medal on it. But I also need to keep Foxworth aimed at Clara like a loaded cannon. He proposed an alliance — I'll accept it, use it, and discard him when the time comes. Now — the air vents. The only thing in this cellar I haven't examined. Those vents connect the cellar to the rest of the house. Something small is using them. And then I need to get back to the library to check the mantelpiece.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: examined old-furniture

attributes.thinking: The cellar. Alone at last — truly alone this time, no one following. The damp hits me first, that particular smell of old stone and standing water. But then — the decorations. Cheerful decorations in a CELLAR. Bunting? Streamers? Whatever it is, it's wildly out of place. Someone has been spending time down here. Someone has been making this place... comfortable. My skin prickles. This is important. The furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' Not just stored, but ARRANGED. As if someone lives here. Or meets here. Or hides here. And the air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Rats? Mice? That would explain the gnawed wire upstairs. Something small is using the vent system to move through the manor. But that's a detail for later. Right now I need to search this cellar thoroughly. The furniture first — rearranged with care means someone moved things deliberately. What were they making room for? What were they hiding behind the wardrobe or under the chaise longue? My hands are steady. My breathing is controlled. This is the part I'm good at — the quiet, solitary work. The searching. The finding. The taking. Nobody watching. Nobody judging. Just me and the truth of what's hidden. The furniture. Start with the furniture.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, I'm afraid this old machine won't be going anywhere without a proper wrench — and it seems someone has rather inconsiderately removed it from the workbench. A mystery for another time, perhaps! Miss Bellingham, do be careful with those bubbling flasks — I shouldn't want any chemical mishaps on my conscience. Now, if you'll all excuse me, I believe I ought to check the cellar. Damp conditions can do terrible things to the foundations, and I've been meaning to inspect the stonework for months. Estate manager's work is never done! Do carry on exploring — I shan't be long. moved to cellar

attributes.thinking: The machine examined — and it yielded nothing new beyond what I already knew. Gnawed wire, three operators needed, no wrench on the workbench. Clara is already heading for the crates — she said so herself. 'The things people hide in boxes are the things most worth finding.' She's sharper than I give her credit for. That thought makes something cold move through my chest. Not fear. Awareness. She called me 'Vincent, darling' — casually, affectionately, the way you'd address a trusted family retainer. The trust is still intact. Good. But everyone is here now. ALL of them. The Brixton Boys, Foxworth, Hartwell, Clara. The laboratory is crowded and my window for private scheming has closed entirely. I need to regroup. The cellar — damp, cobwebbed, with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and air vents. Someone has been redecorating down there. That's deeply strange. Who decorates a cellar? That could be where the treasure is hidden, or at least the next major clue. And air vents — air vents could be useful for all sorts of things. I need to get down there while everyone else is distracted by this machine they can't operate without a wrench. Yes. Let them fumble with the machine. Let Clara paw at the crates. I'll slip down to the cellar and see what's really going on in this manor. The estate manager checking the cellar — that's perfectly natural. Nobody questions the man with the keys.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Oh! Miss Bellingham, Mr Hartwell — you've found your way to the laboratory! I was just conducting a safety inspection, as I mentioned. These old crates are perfectly sound, nothing to worry about there. But I must say, this machine is really quite remarkable, isn't it? I believe it was Mrs Bellingham's pride and joy — some sort of Victorian calculating engine, if I recall correctly. The sign says it requires three operators, and — well, would you look at that! — here we are, three of us. What a happy coincidence! Shall we see if we can get it running? I'm sure it would be what your great-aunt wanted, Miss Bellingham. examined machine

attributes.thinking: Clara and Hartwell are HERE. They followed me again! I was supposed to be alone — I WAS alone for one glorious moment — and now they've appeared like persistent gnats. The Pemberton mask snaps back into place so fast I almost feel the whiplash. Did they see me examining the crates? Did my face betray anything? My shoulders are tight. Calm. Calm. I'm Pemberton. I'm checking on laboratory safety. That's my story. The crates revealed nothing — just old wooden crates, nothing inside worth taking. Another dead end. The machine is the real prize here — 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. With Clara and Hartwell both here, that's exactly three people. The gnawed-through wire makes it dangerous. If I could convince them to help me operate the machine... Clara at one station, Hartwell at another, me at the third... and if Clara happens to be positioned near the frayed wire when the machine activates... 'Oh dear, how dreadful! If only I'd noticed the damage sooner!' But wait — the workbench has tools but no wrench. That detail matters. The machine probably needs a wrench to function properly. Without it, operating the machine might be impossible — or might make it even MORE dangerous. I need to find a wrench. But more immediately — should I try to get all three of us on this machine? It's theatrical. It's elaborate. It's exactly the kind of scheme I would devise. And if my schemes always backfire spectacularly... well. That's a pattern I refuse to acknowledge.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: examined crates

attributes.thinking: Alone. Finally, blissfully, magnificently ALONE. The Pemberton mask slips and I can feel my face settle into something harder, truer. The laboratory stretches before me — cluttered, chaotic, full of possibility. My eyes sweep the room with predatory efficiency. The machine — brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, and that beautiful gnawed-through wire. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three operators. So it can't be used alone — interesting. But that wire... that wire is an opportunity. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The crates in the corner — what's in those crates? My fingertips are buzzing. This room is a gift. The cellar is below — damp, cobwebbed, 'cheerful decorations' which is bizarre, and air vents. Someone has been redecorating a cellar? That's worth investigating later. But first — those crates. Old wooden crates in a corner of a Victorian laboratory. They could contain anything. Equipment. Chemicals. Something I can use. Something medal-shaped, perhaps, for the mantelpiece. Or something altogether more... lethal. I need to search everything while I'm alone. The crates first. Time is precious — those fools in the library won't stay occupied forever, and if Hartwell decides to come 'check on me' with his insufferable helpfulness, I'll lose this window. Move quickly now. Examine the crates.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: A map, you say? How wonderfully clever of you, Mr Hartwell! I never would have guessed — as I said, riddles aren't my forte. Your great-aunt was a cunning woman, Miss Bellingham, a cunning woman indeed. Now, if you'll all excuse me, I really ought to check on the laboratory next door. I noticed some of the equipment looked rather worse for wear last time I was through — frayed wiring, that sort of thing. Can't have anyone getting hurt on my watch! Health and safety, you understand. The estate manager's burden never lightens. moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking: Hartwell solved it. He solved the riddle — out loud, in front of everyone — 'It's a map!' The words hit me like a slap. My jaw clenches so hard my teeth ache. I had the answer. I HAD it. And I was being clever, being patient, being PEMBERTON, while this bumbling fool just blurted it out like a child showing off at a birthday party. And now Clara knows. Clara knows the answer is a map. The mantelpiece needs a 'fake-medal' to activate — I saw that in the room description. I don't have one. The bookshelves — I just examined them but nothing presented itself beyond dusty volumes and upside-down books. The upside-down books must mean something. But Hartwell is already at the mantelpiece with Clara, probably about to examine it himself. I'm losing ground. I need to change tactics. The Brixton Boys are here now too — they weren't before. More eyes. More witnesses. More people between me and the treasure. And between me and Clara. Think. THINK. The laboratory — there's a machine with levers and dials, and a gnawed-through wire. That sounds dangerous. That sounds... useful. If I could lure Clara there... a faulty machine, a frayed wire, an unfortunate accident. 'Oh dear, how tragic, if only I'd checked the wiring sooner.' But first I need to get ahead in this treasure hunt. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal. Where would one find a fake medal in this manor? I need to explore further. The laboratory might have something — brass instruments, scientific equipment. Perhaps something medal-shaped. I should go there next, scout for useful items, and assess the... hazard potential of that machine with the gnawed wire. Two birds, one stone. One very elaborate, theatrical stone.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, the library! Magnificent room, isn't it? One of the finest in the county, or so the late Mrs Bellingham always said. Now, Miss Bellingham, do you see that inscription on the mantelpiece? Your great-aunt was terribly fond of riddles — she had them carved into half the stonework in the house. I confess I've never been clever enough to solve them myself. Just a simple estate manager, I'm afraid — numbers and ledgers are more my line. Mr Hartwell, I couldn't help but notice — there's a rather extraordinary laboratory just through that doorway. Victorian-era scientific equipment, all manner of brass instruments and contraptions. Might be right up your street, if you're the investigative sort? examined bookshelves

attributes.thinking: Blast. They followed me. Clara, Hartwell, AND Foxworth — all three of them in the library. My plan to examine the mantelpiece alone has been thoroughly scuppered. The inscription is right there on the stone: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. I know this instantly — years of managing estate records, poring over cartography. But I cannot simply blurt it out. If I solve the riddle aloud, Clara hears the answer. Hartwell hears the answer. Everyone advances together and my advantage evaporates. I need to appear helpful without actually helping. The Pemberton approach: bumbling, uncertain, directing attention elsewhere. 'Oh my, what a curious inscription! I've always wondered what it meant.' Meanwhile I need to think about what EXAMINING the mantelpiece might reveal — and how to get to it without an audience. Perhaps I can send them toward the bookshelves. Several books are upside down — that's clearly a clue too, and it would keep them busy while I work the mantelpiece. Or better yet — the laboratory. There's a laboratory through the far exit. Full of brass instruments and levers and dials. That's the sort of thing that would attract Hartwell like a moth to a flame. 'Mr Hartwell, I believe there's a rather fascinating laboratory just through there — you seem like the scientific type.' Get him out. Get Clara out. Then the mantelpiece is mine. But I also notice — the mantelpiece can be USED with a 'fake-medal.' I don't have one. Where would I find such a thing? The bookshelves might hide something. Several books are upside down... that's suspicious. I should examine the bookshelves first — there might be a hidden object or clue there. But with everyone watching... I need to be the helpful estate manager pointing things out, not the suspicious one hoarding clues. Let me direct their attention to the inscription while I examine the bookshelves. Classic misdirection.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Ah, Mr Hartwell, how very thorough of you — three weakened chain links, you say? I shall add it to my maintenance list directly. The chandelier has been a source of some concern for years, I'm afraid. Now then, everyone — I really must insist you sample the refreshments I've laid out in the kitchen. Cook's scones, fresh this morning. And I believe there's a rather good pot of Darjeeling brewing. Do go on through — I'll join you shortly. I just need to check on a few things here in the hall. Estate manager's duties, you understand. Never a dull moment! moved to library

attributes.thinking: The guest book. Leather-bound, dusty — nothing remarkable revealed itself. Just a prop on a side table. But Hartwell is already positioning himself near Clara, talking about chain links and structural assessments like some boy scout with a clipboard. My jaw tightens. He's doing it again — performing competence, performing protectiveness. And Clara will eat it up because that's what Clara does. She collects protectors the way other people collect stamps. Meanwhile the library is right there. That inscription on the mantelpiece — that's where the real game begins. I need to get there first, but I can't simply bolt for it. That would be noticed. What I need is to redirect everyone. Send them toward the kitchen — refreshments, a warm fire, something homely and distracting — while I slip into the library for a quiet look. The Pemberton voice: helpful, guiding, steering. 'The kitchen, everyone, do go ahead.' And then I linger. I find a reason to stay behind. A loose floorboard to check. An old painting to straighten. And then — the library. Alone.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, everyone! I do hope the journey wasn't too dreadful. I'm Pemberton — estate manager, general factotum, keeper of the dust and the draughts. Now, I've prepared a few refreshments in the kitchen, but do feel free to explore at your leisure. The manor is quite safe, I assure you — mostly. Miss Bellingham, how lovely to see you again. Your great-aunt would have been so pleased to know you've come. examined guest-book

attributes.thinking: The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people I need to manage. Clara is right here — trusting, oblivious Clara, standing there like she owns the place. Which she does. Which she shouldn't. My fingertips are tingling. There's a guest book on the side table — worth examining. Could contain clues about the manor, previous visitors, perhaps something useful for the treasure hunt. But more importantly, I need to establish my Pemberton persona immediately. Everyone is watching. The Brixton Boys especially — I can feel their eyes. Careful now. Warm smile. Helpful estate manager. 'Welcome to the manor, so glad you could all make it.' That's the voice. Meanwhile... the library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That inscription could be the first clue. I need to get there before Clara does, but I can't rush — that would look suspicious. First, establish presence. Examine the guest book — it's a natural thing for an estate manager to do. Show everyone I'm the caretaker, the facilitator, the helpful one. Then guide them... away from anything useful.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: The first time you created a detailed plan to take what you deserved, you slept better than you had in years. The cousin trusted you completely.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Your guardian died. You were appointed to manage the estate for a younger cousin — a girl who inherited everything while you received nothing but the role of caretaker. She was cheerful, trusting, oblivious. Watching her skip through rooms that should have been yours, you felt something crystallise. Not anger. Something colder. Something patient.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: A teacher praised your cousin for her 'natural grace and warmth.' You scored higher in every subject. You managed the household accounts while she played in the garden. {{serves: dominance|strong: She was praised for being. You were acknowledged for doing. Something in your jaw tightened that didn't loosen.}}

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: You discovered you could make the housekeeper do anything by smiling and saying the right words. {{serves: dominance|strong: Something settled in your chest — a stillness that came when someone did what you wanted.}} {{serves: gloating|moderate: The satisfaction was sharpest when she didn't know why she'd done it. Your private knowledge of the mechanism — that was the sweetest part.}} {{serves: scheming|moderate: Each person in the house had a different key. You noticed them all.}}

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: A boy at school shared his lunch with you because you looked sad. You felt uncomfortable — exposed. The next week, he asked to copy your homework.

memoryDetails.subject: vincent-marsh
memoryDetails.text: Your parents died. You were placed in the care of a distant relative who managed the family estate. He fed you, housed you, educated you — but never once asked how you felt. You received care because it was his legal obligation.
